instructions: Translate each "en" text into the target language and put it in the "ka" field. Use "context" to choose the right meaning. Keep it natural and short; for vocab terms give the dictionary form. Leave the field empty if you are not sure. Do not change "key" or "en".

items.context: B1 n — What you think about something. Example: In my opinion, the film was too long.
B1 n — Something that makes a situation better. Example: One advantage of living here is the clean air.
B1 n — Something that makes a situation worse. Example: The main disadvantage is the cost.
B1 v — To say that something is good or suitable. Example: Can you recommend a good restaurant?
B1 v — To make someone agree to do something by giving reasons. Example: She persuaded me to come with her.
B1 v — To have a different opinion. Example: I'm afraid I disagree with you.
B1 n — A particular way of thinking about something. Example: I understand your point of view.
B1 phr — Used to introduce a contrasting idea. Example: The job is well paid. On the other hand, the hours are long.
B1 adv — In fact; used to correct or add surprising information. Example: I thought he was English, but actually he's Irish.
B1 adv — In a way that is easy to see or understand. Example: Obviously, we need more time.
B1 n — An illegal action that can be punished by law. Example: Crime has fallen in the city centre.
B1 v — To take something that does not belong to you. Example: Someone stole my bike.
B1 n — A rule made by the government. Example: It's against the law to drive without a licence.
B1 n — The group of people who control a country. Example: The government plans to build new schools.
B1 n — An occasion when people vote to choose someone. Example: The next election is in October.
B1 v — To show your choice in an election. Example: Young people should vote.
B1 n — The people living in one area, or a group with shared interests. Example: The library is important for the local community.
B1 n — A person who works without being paid. Example: Volunteers helped clean the beach.
B1 n — An organisation that helps people in need. Example: She gives money to charity every month.
B1 adj — Extremely large. Example: They live in a huge house.
B1 adj — Extremely small. Example: The flat is tiny but cheap.
B1 adj — Extremely surprising and good. Example: The view from the top was amazing.
B1 adj — Very bad or unpleasant. Example: The weather was awful.
B1 adj — Different from what is normal. Example: It's unusual to see snow in April.
B1 adj — Having the usual qualities of a particular type. Example: This is a typical Georgian breakfast.
B1 adj — Easy to recognise because you have seen it before. Example: Her face looks familiar.
B1 adj — Able to be used or obtained. Example: Are there any tickets available?
B1 adj — Right for a particular purpose. Example: This film isn't suitable for children.
B1 adj — Easy, useful or suitable for your plans. Example: Is Monday convenient for you?
B1 adj — Working well without wasting time or energy. Example: The new system is more efficient.
B1 adj — Needed in order to achieve something. Example: Is it necessary to book in advance?
B1 pv — To continue doing something. Example: Carry on with your work.
B1 pv — To take care of someone or something. Example: Can you look after my cat this weekend?
B1 pv — To refuse an offer; to reduce the volume. Example: She turned down the job offer. Please turn down the music.
B1 pv — To delay doing something. Example: Don't put off going to the dentist.
B1 pv — To think of an idea or plan. Example: We need to come up with a solution.
B1 pv — To have none of something left. Example: We've run out of milk.
B1 pv — To start a business or organisation. Example: She set up her own company.
B1 pv — To take action to solve a problem. Example: Who deals with customer complaints?
B1 pv — To find the answer; to do exercise. Example: I can't work out this problem. I work out three times a week.
B1 pv — To recover from an illness or a bad experience. Example: It took her a long time to get over the flu.
B1 pv — To start a new hobby or activity. Example: I've taken up yoga.
B1 pv — To stop working (of a machine or vehicle). Example: Our car broke down on the motorway.
B1 pv — To tell someone a fact or show them something. Example: She pointed out a mistake in my report.
B1 pv — To solve a problem or organise something. Example: I need to sort out my visa.
B1 pv — To arrive, often unexpectedly. Example: He turned up an hour late.
B1 phr — To decide something. Example: We need to make a decision today.
B1 phr — To stop working or doing something for a short time. Example: Let's take a ten-minute break.
B1 phr — To watch, listen to or think about something carefully. Example: Please pay attention to the instructions.
B1 phr — To continue to communicate with someone. Example: Let's keep in touch after the course.
B1 phr — To improve or develop. Example: You're making good progress with your English.
B1 phr — To try as hard as you can. Example: Don't worry about the result. Just do your best.
B1 phr — To try to do something. Example: I've never surfed, but I'd like to have a go.
B1 phr — Used to introduce a new topic in conversation. Example: By the way, have you seen Nino lately?
B1 phr — Used to say that the answer changes according to the situation. Example: 'Are you coming?' 'It depends on the weather.'
B1 phr — Finally, after a long time or a lot of discussion. Example: In the end, we decided to stay at home.
B1 conj — Despite the fact that. Example: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
B1 prep — Without being affected by something. Example: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.
B1 conj — Except if. Example: You won't pass unless you study.
B1 adv — For that reason. Example: The train was cancelled; therefore, we took a bus.
B1 phr — Because of this. Example: It snowed heavily. As a result, schools were closed.
B1 phr — Used to add another point. Example: The hotel has a pool. In addition, there's a free gym.
B1 phr — Used to give an example. Example: Many fruits, for example oranges, contain vitamin C.
B1 adv — In place of someone or something. Example: There was no coffee, so I had tea instead.
B1 adv — In the end, after a long time. Example: After many tries, he eventually passed his driving test.
B1 adv — Not long ago. Example: I've recently started a new job.
B1 adv — At the present time, compared with the past. Example: Nowadays, most people pay by card.
B1 n — A person who formally asks for a job or a place on a course. Example: There were over a hundred applicants for the job.
B1 n — Extra time that you work after your usual hours. Example: She did ten hours of overtime last week.
B1 n — Money paid to a worker, usually every week or every hour. Example: The minimum wage went up this year.
B1 n — Money paid regularly to someone who has stopped working because of age. Example: My grandfather lives on his pension.
B1 v — To employ someone; also, to pay to use something for a short time. Example: The company is hiring new staff.
B1 n — A type of job that needs special training or education. Example: Teaching is a demanding profession.
B1 n — A piece of work given to a student. Example: The history assignment is due on Friday.
B1 n — Money given to a student to help pay for their studies. Example: She won a scholarship to study in Canada.
B1 n — Teaching, or the money paid for being taught. Example: University tuition fees have risen.
B1 v — To complete a university or college degree. Example: He graduated in law last year.
B1 n — A mark that shows the quality of a student's work. Example: She got the highest grade in the class.
B1 n — One of the main parts of a book. Example: Read the first two chapters for homework.
B1 n — The title of a newspaper story, printed in large letters. Example: The scandal made the headlines.
B1 v — To send out a programme on television or radio. Example: The match will be broadcast live.
B1 v — To produce a book, magazine or article for people to buy or read. Example: The results will be published next month.
B1 v — To repeat the exact words that someone else said or wrote. Example: The article quoted the minister directly.
B1 n — A long period with little or no rain. Example: The drought destroyed most of the crops.
B1 n — A large amount of water covering an area that is usually dry. Example: The floods forced hundreds of families to leave their homes.
B1 adj — Connected with the countryside, not towns. Example: Many young people leave rural areas for the city.
B1 n — The usual way and order in which you do things. Example: Exercise is part of my morning routine.
B1 n — Free time when you are not working. Example: What do you do in your leisure time?
B1 n — All the people who live together in one home. Example: Most households now have internet access.
B1 n — The feeling that you want to eat. Example: Swimming always gives me a good appetite.
B1 adj — Old; a polite word for old people. Example: She looks after her elderly parents.
B1 v — To stop being angry with someone who has done something wrong. Example: I can't forgive him for lying to me.
B1 v — To say that someone is responsible for something bad. Example: Don't blame me — it wasn't my idea.
B1 n — A feeling of being sorry for someone who is unhappy. Example: We send our sympathy to the family.
B1 adj — Always supporting a friend, a belief or an organisation. Example: He has been a loyal friend for years.
B1 n — A feeling of pleasure because of something you or people close to you have done. Example: She spoke about her son with pride.
B1 n — The line that separates two countries. Example: We crossed the border into Turkey.
B1 n — The way from one place to another. Example: What's the quickest route to the airport?
B1 adj — Far away from towns and other people. Example: They live in a remote mountain village.
B1 n — An area where people live on the edge of a city. Example: We moved to a quiet suburb.
B1 v — To put software or equipment in place so that it is ready to use. Example: You need to install the app first.
B1 adj — Working without wires, using radio signals. Example: Is there wireless internet in the hotel?
B1 adj — Created by computers or existing online rather than physically. Example: We had a virtual meeting with the team in Berlin.
B1 n — Money that you earn or receive regularly. Example: Rent takes half of my income.
B1 n — An amount of money paid for a service or to join something. Example: There's no entrance fee for students.
B1 n — Money spent on something. Example: Travel expenses will be paid by the company.
B1 n — Money paid as the first part of a payment, or put into a bank account. Example: We paid a deposit of 500 lari for the flat.
B1 n — An arrangement in which you pay a company that will pay you if something bad happens. Example: Don't travel without health insurance.
B1 n — A strong feeling that something is true. Example: It's a common belief that carrots help you see in the dark.
B1 n — A feeling of not being sure. Example: I have my doubts about his plan.
B1 n — A discussion in which people express different opinions. Example: There's a lively debate about school uniforms.
B1 n — A person who legally belongs to a country. Example: She became a British citizen last year.
B1 n — A person who has been hurt or killed, or who has suffered because of something. Example: The victims of the flood received help.
B1 adj — Having a strong wish to be successful. Example: She's very ambitious and wants to run her own company.
B1 adj — Wanting to know or learn about something. Example: Children are naturally curious.
B1 adj — Feeling or showing thanks. Example: I'm really grateful for your help.
B1 adj — Not giving enough attention to what you are doing. Example: It was a careless mistake.
B2 phr — To give reasons why you believe something is true. Example: She argues that schools should start later.
B2 v — To say that something is true, without proof. Example: The company claims its product is eco-friendly.
B2 v — To believe something is true without checking. Example: I assumed you'd already left.
B2 v — To accept that something is true. Example: He acknowledged that he had made a mistake.
B2 v — To say the opposite of what someone has said; to disagree with facts. Example: The results contradict earlier research.
B2 adj — Causing a lot of disagreement. Example: The new law is highly controversial.
B2 adj — Unfairly preferring one side. Example: The article was clearly biased.
B2 n — An argument against another argument. Example: A good essay considers counter-arguments.
B2 phr — Partly, but not completely. Example: I agree with you to some extent.
B2 phr — Used to introduce a point that contrasts with what you have just said. Example: It's an expensive city. Having said that, the salaries are high.
B2 phr — Used to say that something is useful or good to do. Example: It's worth visiting the old town.
B2 n — The system of trade, industry and money in a country. Example: Tourism is important for the economy.
B2 adj — Relating to trade, industry and money. Example: The country is facing economic problems.
B2 n — A situation where businesses try to be more successful than others. Example: There is strong competition between the two airlines.
B2 v — To start selling a new product or begin an activity. Example: They launched the new phone in May.
B2 v — To discuss something to reach an agreement. Example: We negotiated a better price.
B2 v — To become less in amount or quality. Example: Sales have declined this year.
B2 n — An increase in size or amount. Example: The country has seen rapid economic growth.
B2 n — A product name made by a particular company. Example: Which brand of coffee do you buy?
B2 n — A person who buys goods or services. Example: Consumers are becoming more environmentally aware.
B2 n — A test done to learn something or prove an idea. Example: Scientists carried out an experiment on mice.
B2 n — The act of finding something for the first time. Example: The discovery of penicillin saved millions of lives.
B2 n — An idea that tries to explain something. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution.
B2 n — Facts and numbers collected for study. Example: We analysed data from 2,000 patients.
B2 v — To examine something in detail. Example: The samples are being analysed in a laboratory.
B2 n — An important new discovery or development. Example: Scientists have made a breakthrough in cancer research.
B2 adj — Made by people, not natural. Example: The drink contains artificial colours.
B2 adj — Relating to genes. Example: The disease has a genetic cause.
B2 adj — Able to be replaced naturally. Example: Wind and solar are renewable energy sources.
B2 n — Gas or other substances sent into the air. Example: Cars produce harmful emissions.
B2 n — The right to keep your personal life private. Example: Social media raises concerns about privacy.
B2 n — Protection of computer systems from attacks. Example: Banks spend a lot on cyber security.
B2 n — People living together in organised communities. Example: Technology has changed society.
